content: The air system at Murry Bergtraum High School, located approximately three-fourths of a mile east of the World Trade Center site, was severely impacted and damaged by debris and dust from the 9/11 attacks. This contamination was not adequately addressed, as the school’s central air system was not thoroughly cleaned in the years following the attacks. As a result, several teachers, particularly those in the business department, and students have developed asthma and other respiratory conditions due to prolonged exposure to polluted air. On January 30, 2007, workers from Ground Zero, along with advocacy groups such as the Sierra Club and Unsung Heroes Helping Heroes, gathered at the Ground Zero site to protest and demand increased financial support for workers who had fallen ill due to their exposure to hazardous conditions during the cleanup. They criticized President George W. Bush’s promise of $25 million in aid as insufficient. John Sferazo, a Long Island ironworker, questioned why it had taken the President over five years to meet with them. Local residents also joined the protest. Mariama James, who lived just blocks from Ground Zero, reported becoming ill after cleaning debris and dust from her apartment. She emphasized that recovery workers were not the only ones affected by the disaster, stating that others also required medical treatment and ongoing monitoring. By September 2007, the number of plaintiffs in related lawsuits had reached 10,000. One individual who initiated a lawsuit on behalf of a sick police officer noted that the case was initially avoided by many due to fears of being perceived as unpatriotic for criticizing the cleanup efforts or the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA). Several legislative efforts were introduced in Congress to address the health impacts of the 9/11 attacks. These included the Remember 9/11 Health Act, sponsored by Congresswoman Carolyn Maloney, and the James Zadroga Act, sponsored by Senator Bob Menendez and Congresswoman Maloney. On September 13, 2006, a $9 billion treatment program was proposed to assist those suffering from the long-term effects of exposure to Ground Zero dust and fumes. Residents of Lower Manhattan and Brooklyn filed a 111-page lawsuit against the EPA, accusing the agency of misleading the public about the safety of air and dust in the aftermath of the attacks. Jenna Orkin, a Brooklyn resident and member of the World Trade Center Environmental Organization, played a significant role in this legal effort. On February 2, 2006, Federal Court Judge Deborah Batts issued an 83-page statement allowing the case to proceed, citing sufficient grounds for the lawsuit. She also denied granting immunity to former EPA Director Christine Todd Whitman, who was among the defendants. Legal proceedings began on December 10, 2007, to determine the responsibility of government officials in the aftermath of the 9/11 attacks. Plaintiffs alleged that Whitman was at fault for falsely assuring the public that the air in downtown New York was safe following the attacks.
